name: Priya Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for joining me, Priya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no links to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and everything you say stays confidential. Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We run Mill Lane Farm, 120 hectares, with 12,000 free-range laying hens and field vegetables, mostly carrots and leeks. I'm up at five to check the hen houses, though half of that is now on a screen: temperature, water, egg counts. Then I'm on the phone to the supermarket buyer or packing veg boxes, and I've seven staff to keep happy. My husband Kofi runs a car repair garage in town, so the kids, Ama and Daniel, get dropped at school by whoever's less muddy.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use AI in that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day, all day. I use it to plan rotations, check the hens' data for early signs of disease, and write the boring emails to the buyer. I don't love AI, I love not doing paperwork at eleven at night, and AI gets me that. I usually try new kit before the neighbours do, and sometimes I get burned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a good tool, not a miracle. I'd probably post that on the growers' forum. Nobody would argue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it'd suit me fine. I've already got the gains from it, the paperwork, the data. It means the big operators don't get a huge leap on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing. I'd still trial things, like a robot to weed the carrot beds if one came along that actually worked. I'd put more energy into growing the veg box scheme, because that's where the margin is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a little bored.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd regret?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The weeding, honestly. Hand-weeding carrots is brutal, and I can never get enough people for it. I'd swap every clever app on my phone for one robot that can weed a carrot bed without killing the carrots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the staff think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd shrug. Marta, who runs the packing shed, is more interested in whether we get a new conveyor. The weeding crew would be glad to keep the work, it's seasonal money they count on.

S0.say: I'd say on the growers' forum that AI is a good tool, not a miracle. I don't think anyone would argue.
S0.think: Privately it'd suit me fine, since I already get the paperwork and data gains. It also means the big operators don't leap ahead of me.
S0.do: Keeps going as she is while still trialling any carrot-weeding robot that actually works. Puts more energy into growing the veg box scheme, where the margin is.
S0.quote: I'd swap every clever app on my phone for one robot that can weed a carrot bed without killing the carrots.
S0.fieldNote: Priya is a practical early adopter who uses AI to escape late-night paperwork rather than out of love for it. Her one wish is a weeding robot, because she can't find enough hands for the carrot beds. She sees a plateau as levelling the field against big operators.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for small farms to punch above their weight, if they move early. I'd also say we need decent training so people aren't left behind. I'd say it on the forum and at the growers' association.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd come out ahead. I'm already set up for it. My worry is the weeding crew, who are local mums and students, and what they do when a robot does their summer work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a weeding robot for the carrots in the first spring, around 70,000, partly from savings and partly a loan. I'd put cameras on the egg grading line. I'd offer the weeding crew other work, packing veg boxes or doing farm-gate sales, because the box scheme would grow. And I'd keep testing the AI tools for hen health.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly positive. A bit of guilt about the weeders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You call it guilt. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because some of them have worked for me for eight summers and they need that money for school uniforms. I'd be buying a robot to do the job I spent years begging people to do, and then telling them I don't need them. That's not nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your plans if the robot didn't work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd send it back, if I could, or sell it on. I've been burned before with a drone that never flew straight. I'd still try it, though.

S1.say: I'd say this is a chance for small farms to punch above their weight if they move early, as long as there's decent training so nobody's left behind. I'd say it on the forum and at the growers' association.
S1.think: Privately I think I'd come out ahead because I'm already set up for it. My worry is the local weeding crew, mostly mums and students, who'd lose summer work.
S1.do: Buys a carrot-weeding robot in the first spring for about 70,000 from savings and a loan, and adds cameras to the egg grading line. Offers the weeding crew packing or farm-gate sales work as the veg box scheme grows.
S1.feel: Mostly positive, with some guilt about the weeding crew.
S1.quote: I'd be buying a robot to do the job I spent years begging people to do, and then telling them I don't need them.
S1.fieldNote: Priya moves first and expects to win, but she feels guilty about replacing seasonal workers she once begged to come. She offers them other roles tied to the growing box scheme. She's honest that she's been burned by technology before and would try anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say everyone's going to have to move fast and help each other. I wouldn't panic in public. I'd say farmers who adapt will be fine, and the government needs to help those who can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be more worried than I'd say. My advantage is being early, and in two years everyone's early. The supermarket would cut prices the moment big robot farms flood them with eggs, and that's my main contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd automate everything I could in the first six months, weeding, grading, packing. I'd build up cash, because the egg price could fall hard. And I'd grow the veg box scheme and the farm shop, because people still want to buy from a face they know. Kofi's garage might need my help too, if self-driving cars hit his trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. In control, but only just.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people want to buy from a face they know. Are you sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'm not sure. It's a hope. If robots can grow everything cheaper, then the only thing I'm really selling is my face at the farm gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ama and Daniel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That things are changing fast but we're ready. Ama's ten and she'd ask if the hens would still know me. I'd tell her yes, and I'd believe it.

S2.say: I'd say everyone needs to move fast and help each other, without panicking in public. I'd say farmers who adapt will be fine and the government should help those who can't.
S2.think: Privately I'm more worried than I'd say, because my edge is being early and in two years everyone is early. The supermarket would cut egg prices when robot farms flood the market.
S2.do: Automates weeding, grading and packing within six months and builds a cash buffer against an egg price collapse. Grows the veg box scheme and farm shop as a second income, and helps Kofi if self-driving cars hit his garage.
S2.feel: Anxious and in control, but only just.
S2.quote: If robots can grow everything cheaper, then the only thing I'm really selling is my face at the farm gate.
S2.fieldNote: Priya's say and think split clearly here: calm in public, privately worried that her early-mover edge disappears. Her fallback is the farm gate, which she admits is a hope rather than a certainty. She notices that Kofi's garage is exposed too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty if you start now, and I'd start now. I'd be on the forum sharing what I'd learned. I'd say the government should help farmers and workers retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is my sweet spot. I'd be ahead again, but with time to build things the robots can't, like the farm shop and the box scheme. I'd sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd automate the carrots and grading, then the packing by year two. I'd turn the old barn into a proper farm shop with a café, which costs about 150,000 and I'd borrow some of it. I'd train Marta to manage the shop. And Kofi and I would look at his garage switching to electric vehicle repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little, but mostly I'd be excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A café is quite a different business. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's about people, and nobody's going to drive out of town to be served coffee by a robot. In five years I'd want our farm to be a place people visit, not just a place eggs come from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The loan, if the café flops. And whether Kofi can switch fast enough. He's good with his hands, but he's not one for screens.

S3.say: I'd say five years is plenty if you start now, and I'd share what I learned on the growers' forum. I'd say the government should help farmers and workers retrain.
S3.think: Privately five years is my sweet spot: I'd be ahead again and have time to build things robots can't, like the shop and box scheme. I'd sleep fine.
S3.do: Automates the carrots and grading in year one and packing by year two. Converts the old barn into a farm shop and café for about 150,000, partly borrowed, trains Marta to manage it, and helps Kofi shift his garage to electric vehicle repairs.
S3.feel: A little uneasy but mostly excited.
S3.quote: In five years I'd want our farm to be a place people visit, not just a place eggs come from.
S3.fieldNote: Five years is the timeline Priya likes best, because it rewards early movers without leaving everyone early. Her plan shifts towards a people business, a café and shop. Her lingering worries are the loan and her husband's slower adaptation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway and there's no excuse not to plan. I'd say it on the forum and I'd run a day for local growers to see what we'd done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine, more than fine. I'd be 53, with the farm automated, the shop running and the mortgage gone. I'd want to make sure the kids learned something useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd automate step by step, a bit each year as prices drop. I'd build the shop and café over three or four years without a loan. I'd put money aside for Ama and Daniel's studies and steer them, gently, towards things with people in them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are you worried you'd wait too long with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not me. I'd worry I'd move too early and buy the expensive version. With ten years, my problem isn't being late, it's paying first-buyer prices for kit that's half the price two years later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Daniel, who'd be seventeen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn to fix things and talk to people. Kofi says the same. Daniel would probably want to build robots, knowing him, and that's fine too.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long runway and there's no excuse not to plan. I'd say so on the forum and host a day for local growers to see what we'd done.
S4.think: Privately I'd be more than fine at 53, with the farm automated, the shop running and the mortgage gone. I'd want the kids to learn something useful.
S4.do: Automates step by step as prices drop and builds the shop and café over three or four years without a loan. Saves for Ama and Daniel's studies and gently steers them towards work with people in it.
S4.feel: Calm, because it's a long runway.
S4.quote: With ten years, my problem isn't being late, it's paying first-buyer prices for kit that's half the price two years later.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Priya's worry flips from being late to buying too early at high prices. She plans to avoid debt this time and pay for the café from earnings. Her advice to her son comes straight from her own life: fix things and talk to people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my edge disappears and the supermarket would squeeze us. What would help is a fair floor on what the supermarkets can pay farmers, and short, cheap training for my staff so they can move into the shop and the café.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the hens. People forget farms are full of animals. Whatever happens, somebody's got to care whether they're well, and I don't want that to be just a number on a screen.

headlineQuote: I don't love AI, I love not doing paperwork at eleven at night, and AI gets me that.
portrait: Priya Mensah is 43 and runs Mill Lane Farm, with 12,000 free-range hens, field vegetables and a veg box scheme, employing seven staff. She uses AI every day, mainly to escape late-night paperwork, and usually tries new kit before her neighbours. She's pragmatic and moves first in every scenario, buying weeding robots and building a farm shop and café as the human side of the business. She's calm in most pictures, anxious only with AGI in two years when everyone becomes an early mover, and with ten years her worry is buying too early.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years, because her advantage of moving early would vanish and the supermarket would squeeze egg prices.
whatWouldHelp: A fair floor on what supermarkets pay farmers, and short, cheap training so her staff can move into the shop and café.
